title: Great Rivers
objective: After this level you can compare the Nile, the Amazon and other great rivers by length and flow.
summary: The Nile is usually ranked longest; the Amazon carries the most water, about a fifth of Earth's runoff. Every river drains a watershed, and you're standing in one.

cards.headline: Which river is the longest? That depends where you think it starts.
cards.body: The Nile and the Amazon have traded blows over first place for years. The fight isn't about a better tape measure. Experts disagree about exactly where a river starts and ends.

items.label: Nile
points: Flows north into the Mediterranean Sea

items.label: Amazon
points: Carries about a fifth of the water running off Earth
Largest river system: biggest basin, biggest flow

cards.headline: Where does a river begin?
cards.body: Some researchers argue the Amazon is actually longer than the Nile. The trouble is the endpoints. Experts disagree about exactly where a river starts and ends, and a different choice changes the answer. So the Nile keeps the length crown, with an asterisk. The flow crown isn't close: the Amazon is the world's largest river system.

cards.headline: You're standing in a watershed
cards.body: All of the Amazon's water comes from its watershed, or drainage basin: the area of land that drains all its streams and rainfall to one outlet. The Amazon's basin is the biggest on Earth. And you live in one too. Everyone standing on land is standing in a watershed. The rain on your street already knows which river it's headed for.

mascot.line: Look down. Congratulations, you are in a watershed. Everyone is. It is the least exclusive club on Earth.

cards.headline: Great rivers: compared
learned: The Nile, about 6,650 km, is usually ranked longest
The Amazon is at least 6,400 km and carries the most water
River lengths depend on where you say they start
A watershed drains to one outlet
Everyone on land stands in a watershed

questions.prompt: Which river is usually ranked the world's longest?

options.label: The Amazon
options.rationale: It carries the most water, but it is usually ranked second in length.

options.label: The Mississippi
options.rationale: Much shorter than the Nile and the Amazon.

options.label: The Yellow River
options.rationale: It is long, but not the longest.

questions.explanation: The Nile, about 6,650 km long, is usually ranked longest, though some researchers argue for the Amazon.

questions.prompt: Why do experts still argue over whether the Nile or the Amazon is longer?

options.label: Both rivers change length every year
options.rationale: The rivers are not the issue; the endpoints are.

options.label: Nobody has ever measured them
options.rationale: Both have been measured many times.

options.label: They disagree about where each river starts and ends
The Amazon is too wide to measure

questions.explanation: Choosing a river's start and end points is a judgment call, and different choices give different lengths.

questions.prompt: From Level 21: gravity pulls rain back across the land. What decides which river the rain on your street ends up in?

options.label: The nearest ocean current
options.rationale: Currents work at sea, not on your street.

options.label: The watershed you are standing in
How far you are from the Equator
options.rationale: Latitude does not decide where rain drains.

options.label: The river's length
options.rationale: Length does not pull in rain.

questions.explanation: A watershed is the land that drains all its streams and rainfall to one outlet, and everyone on land stands in one.
